episodes.title_en: The Bowl That Measured the Rain
episodes.summary_en: Hoya follows the Joseon crown prince's rain experiments to the 1442 rain gauge, the cheugugi, and meets the only Joseon rain-gauge vessel known to survive.
learning_goals: Recognize and say 비 (bi, rain) and the short sentence 비가 와요 (It's raining).
Know that a 1441 royal record describes the crown prince (later King Munjong) testing rain with a metal vessel, and that the device was named 측우기 in 1442.
Understand that officials measured rain with a standard ruler and kept written records across the provinces.
Know that the only Joseon rain gauge vessel known to survive was made in 1837 and is a National Treasure.

scenes.narration_en: Pitter-patter! Hoya the tiger holds out a paw to catch the raindrops. "In Korean, rain is 비," he says. "Long ago, the Joseon kingdom found a clever way to measure rain. Let's go and see!"
scenes.illustration: A small, friendly tiger cub in a light vest stands in gentle rain holding out one paw; soft gray clouds and a tiled-roof Korean house behind him.

scenes.narration_en: A royal record from 1441 says the crown prince, the king's son who later became King Munjong, worried about drought. After each rain, he dug into the ground to see how deep the water had soaked in.
scenes.illustration: A young Joseon crown prince in a red robe kneels in a palace garden beside a small hole, looking at damp soil; a dry field in the distance.

scenes.narration_en: But soil can be dry or damp, so digging could not show exactly how much rain had fallen. So he had a vessel cast from copper and placed in the palace to collect the rainwater.
scenes.illustration: A plain metal cylinder standing in a palace courtyard catching rain, while the prince watches from under the wooden eaves.

scenes.narration_en: In 1442, in King Sejong's reign, a standard rain gauge was named 측우기, 'rain-measuring device.' It stood on a stand at the royal observatory office. After each rain, an official measured the water with a standard ruler and wrote it down.
scenes.illustration: A Joseon official in a black hat dips a slim wooden ruler into a metal rain gauge on a square stone stand; a brush and a record book lie beside him.

scenes.narration_en: Rain gauges and rulers were sent to every province. Local towns could make their gauges from pottery, set them on a stand in a courtyard, measure each rain, and report it to the king.
scenes.illustration: A pottery rain gauge on a stone stand in a country government courtyard; a local magistrate measures with a bamboo ruler; green hills behind.

scenes.narration_en: Joseon sent rain gauges across the land, but only one gauge itself is known to survive today: the rain gauge of the Chungcheong provincial office in Gongju. It was made of bronze in 1837 and is a National Treasure.
scenes.illustration: A bronze cylindrical rain gauge made of three stacked sections, displayed on a museum pedestal under a soft spotlight; Hoya gazes up in wonder.

scenes.narration_en: Today it is kept at the National Meteorological Museum of Korea in Seoul. Hoya grins and points at the sky. "Next time it rains, you can say it in Korean: 비가 와요!"
scenes.illustration: Hoya under a small paper umbrella, pointing happily at the rainy sky in front of a modest museum building.

facts.claim_en: A Sejong Sillok entry dated 1441 (Sejong year 23, 4th lunar month, 29th day) records that the crown prince, worried about drought, used to dig into the ground after rain to see how far the water had soaked in, and because this did not show the exact amount, had a vessel cast from copper (銅) and placed in the palace to measure the rainwater it collected. The crown prince at that time later became King Munjong.
facts.claim_ko: 『세종실록』 세종 23년(1441) 4월 29일 기사에 따르면, 세자는 가뭄을 걱정하여 비가 온 뒤마다 땅을 파서 빗물이 스며든 정도를 살폈으나 정확히 알 수 없었으므로, 구리를 부어 그릇을 만들어 궁중에 두고 그릇에 고인 빗물의 양을 재어 보았다. 이 세자는 훗날의 문종이다.

sources.title: 세종실록 92권, 세종 23년(1441) 4월 29일 을미 1번째 기사 「황우의 변에 대해 승정원에 전지하다」
sources.quote_or_locator: 국역: "근년 이래로 세자가 가뭄을 근심하여, 비가 올 때마다 젖어 들어 간 푼수[分數]를 땅을 파고 보았었다. 그러나 적확하게 비가 온 푼수를 알지 못하였으므로, 구리를 부어 그릇을 만들고는 궁중(宮中)에 두어 빗물이 그릇에 괴인 푼수를 실험하였는데" / 원문: 世子憂旱, 每當雨後, 入土分數, 掘地見之。然未可的知分數, 故鑄銅爲器, 置於宮中

sources.title: 통영 측우대
sources.quote_or_locator: 내용: "측우기의 제도는 1441년(세종 23)에 당시 왕세자였던 문종의 주도하에 만들어졌지만 임진왜란 이후 그 제도가 쇠잔해졌다가"

facts.claim_en: A Sejong Sillok record of a Ministry of Revenue (Hojo) proposal states that soil differs in dryness and dampness, so the depth to which rain soaks into the ground is hard to know.
facts.claim_ko: 『세종실록』에 실린 호조의 건의에 따르면, 흙의 마르고 젖은 정도가 같지 않아 빗물이 흙 속으로 스며든 깊이를 알기 어렵다.

sources.title: 세종실록 93권, 세종 23년(1441) 8월 18일 임오 4번째 기사 「호조에서 서운관에 측우기를 설치할 것을 건의하다」
sources.quote_or_locator: 국역: "토성(土性)의 조습(燥濕)이 같지 아니하고, 흙속으로 스며 든 천심(淺深)도 역시 알기 어렵사오니, 청하옵건대, 서운관(書雲觀)에 대(臺)를 짓고 쇠로 그릇을 부어 만들되 … 대(臺) 위에 올려 놓고 비를 받아"

sources.title: 6) 측우기의 발명과 농업기상학의 발달 (신편 한국사 27권 조선 초기의 문화 Ⅱ > Ⅰ. 과학 > 2. 천문 기상학)
sources.quote_or_locator: "빗물이 땅 속에 스며드는 깊이는 땅이 말랐을 때와 젖었을 때에 따라서 차이가 심하게 드러나기 때문이다."

facts.claim_en: In 1442 (Sejong year 24), a cast-metal instrument was named 측우기 (cheugugi, 'rain-measuring instrument'). In the capital it was placed on a stand at the Seoun-gwan (the royal office for astronomy and weather), and after each rain an official measured the water depth with a standard ruler (jucheok) and recorded it.
facts.claim_ko: 1442년(세종 24) 쇠로 주조한 기구에 측우기라는 이름을 붙였다. 서울에서는 서운관에 대를 만들어 측우기를 그 위에 두고, 비가 온 뒤마다 관원이 주척으로 물의 깊이를 재어 기록하였다.

sources.title: 세종실록 96권, 세종 24년(1442) 5월 8일 정묘 1번째 기사 「호조에서 우량을 측정하는 일에 관해 아뢰다」
sources.quote_or_locator: 국역: "서울에서는 쇠를 주조(鑄造)하여 기구(器具)를 만들어 명칭을 측우기(測雨器)라 하니 … 서운관(書雲觀)에 대(臺)를 만들어 측우기를 대(臺) 위에 두고 매양 비가 온 후에는 본관(本觀)의 관원이 친히 비가 내린 상황을 보고는, 주척(周尺)으로써 물의 깊고 얕은 것을 측량하여 … 상세히 써서 … 기록해 둘 것이며"

sources.title: 국보 공주 충청감영 측우기 (Rain Gauge of Chungcheong Provincial Office, Gongju)
sources.quote_or_locator: "1442년(세종 24)에 발명된 측우기는 … 땅에 스며든 물의 깊이를 측정하던 이전의 비합리적인 강우 측정방식에서 벗어나 본격적으로 강수량을 정량적으로 측정 가능케 한 발명품"

facts.claim_en: Cast-metal rain gauges and standard rulers were sent from the capital to each province; local offices could make gauges of porcelain or earthenware, place them on a stand in the courtyard of the official guesthouse (gaeksa), and the magistrate measured each rain, reported it to the king and kept a record.
facts.claim_ko: 중앙에서 쇠로 주조한 측우기와 주척을 각 도에 보냈고, 각 고을은 자기나 와기로 측우기를 구워 만들어 객사 뜰의 대 위에 두었으며, 수령이 비가 온 뒤 물의 깊이를 재어 임금에게 보고하고 기록하였다.

sources.title: 세종실록 96권, 세종 24년(1442) 5월 8일 정묘 1번째 기사 「호조에서 우량을 측정하는 일에 관해 아뢰다」
sources.quote_or_locator: 국역: "외방(外方)에서는 쇠로써 주조(鑄造)한 측우기(測雨器)와 주척(周尺) 매 1건(件)을 각도(各道)에 보내어, 각 고을로 하여금 … 혹은 자기(磁器)든지 혹은 와기(瓦器)든지 적당한 데에 따라 구워 만들고, 객사(客舍)의 뜰 가운데에 대(臺)를 만들어 측우기를 대(臺) 위에 두도록 하며 … 수령(守令)이 친히 … 계문(啓聞)하고 기록해 두어서"

sources.title: 국보 공주 충청감영 측우기 (Rain Gauge of Chungcheong Provincial Office, Gongju)
sources.quote_or_locator: "조선시대에는 중앙정부에서 측우기를 제작해 전국의 감영에 보냈기 때문에 여러 점이 만들어졌으리라 예상되지만, 지금까지 ‘공주 충청감영 측우기’만 유일하게 알려져 있다."

sources.title: 공주 충청감영 측우기
sources.quote_or_locator: "조선 세종 때 반포되고 영조 때 개정된 우량 관측제도에 의하면, 전국 팔도의 감영(監營)에 측우기를 설치하여 강우량을 측정, 보고하도록 했다."

facts.claim_en: The Rain Gauge of Chungcheong Provincial Office, Gongju (공주 충청감영 측우기), made of bronze in 1837 (Heonjong year 3), is the only Joseon-period rain gauge vessel known to survive, and it is designated a National Treasure. (Several stone bases/stands on which gauges were set also survive, but no other gauge vessel.)
facts.claim_ko: 공주 충청감영 측우기는 1837년(헌종 3)에 청동으로 만든 것으로, 현재까지 알려진 유일한 조선시대 측우기(빗물을 받는 그릇)이며 국보로 지정되어 있다. 측우기를 올려 두던 대석(臺石)은 몇 기가 남아 있다.

sources.title: 국보 공주 충청감영 측우기 (Rain Gauge of Chungcheong Provincial Office, Gongju)
sources.quote_or_locator: "국보 ‘공주 충청감영 측우기(公州 忠淸監營 測雨器)’는 1837년(헌종 3)에 제작된 것으로, 측우대는 없고 측우기만 전해오고 있다. … 지금까지 ‘공주 충청감영 측우기’만 유일하게 알려져 있다." / 지정일 2020.02.27

sources.title: 공주 충청감영 측우기
sources.quote_or_locator: "청동으로 제작된 이 측우기는 표면에 새겨진 “도광정유제(道光丁酉製)”라는 글귀를 통해 1837년(헌종 3)에 제작되었음을 알 수 있다." / "빗물을 담는 그릇으로 현존하는 것은 금영 측우기가 유일하다." / 종목: 국보(2020년 02월 27일 지정) / 현황: "측우기를 설치했던 대석(臺石)은 몇 기가 남아 있지만" (the page continues that the vessel survives only as the 금영 측우기).

episodes.notes: Attribution: popular retellings often say Jang Yeong-sil invented the rain gauge, but the Sejong Sillok (1441-04-29, lunar) credits the crown prince's (later King Munjong's) experiments and encykorea's 통영 측우대 entry says the system was made under the crown prince's lead; Jang Yeong-sil is therefore not mentioned. Deliberately omitted: the KHS description's comparative claim that the cheugugi was the world's first scientific rain gauge, about 200 years before the West (priority claims are contested); the 1441-08-18 proposal's dimensions and the 1442 standard size (1 cheok 5 chon by 7 chon); the Gongju gauge's removal to Japan (KHS: c.1915; encykorea: early 1910s) and return in 1971 (colonial-era history is out of scope); the 1770/1771 revival under King Yeongjo (sources differ on the year). Materials: the Sillok uses 銅 (copper/bronze) for the crown prince's 1441 vessel and 鐵 (cast metal/iron) for the 1442 standard, so narration says 'copper' and 'metal' respectively; the Gongju gauge is bronze (encykorea). All Sillok dates are lunar. Theme set to 'crafts' to match BP04/BP05 Pillar E (E3 측우기). REVISION: (a) Scene 6/summary/learning goal now say only one gauge VESSEL survives; stone stands (대석/측우대) also survive (encykorea E0007902; Tongyeong stand is a Treasure, E0068941). (b) Museum English name 'National Meteorological Museum of Korea' taken from the museum's own website footer (science.kma.go.kr/museum/); the KHS portal lists only the Korean name. (c) Romanization of 서운관 is Seoun-gwan (seo-un-gwan); 'Seounwan' (proposed by one fact-check) would transcribe 서운완, so it was not adopted. (d) Second source added for f2 (신편한국사 via 우리역사넷); new sources accessed 2026-10-10.

episodes.title_en: The Sky-Facing Pot That Told the Time
episodes.summary_en: Hoya discovers King Sejong's bowl-shaped sundials, set beside busy streets in 1434 with animal pictures so that people who could not read could still tell the time.
learning_goals: Recognize and say 해 (hae, sun), 그림자 (geurimja, shadow) and the question 지금 몇 시예요? (What time is it now?).
Explain that the angbuilgu shows the time of day and the time of year from the sun's shadow.
Know that in 1434 sundials were placed beside busy roads and used animal pictures for people who could not read.
Know that Sejong-era sundials do not survive; the ones we see today were made later in Joseon.

scenes.narration_en: Hoya squints up at the bright sky. "In Korean, the sun is 해," he says. "When the sun shines, things cast shadows. In Joseon, people used the sun's shadow to tell the time!"
scenes.illustration: Hoya shading his eyes under a bright sun, his small shadow stretching across the stone paving of a palace courtyard.

scenes.narration_en: In 1434, in King Sejong's reign, a new sundial was set up. Its bowl was round and hollow, like a cooking pot looking up at the sky, so it was called 앙부일구, the 'upward-facing pot sundial.'
scenes.illustration: A bronze bowl-shaped sundial on four short legs, its open side facing a clear blue sky, a slim pointer inside the bowl.

scenes.narration_en: A pointed needle inside the bowl casts a shadow. Some lines show the time of day, and other lines show the time of year. Where the shadow falls tells you both!
scenes.illustration: Close-up of the inside of the sundial bowl: a thin needle casts a dark shadow across a grid of curved lines; no writing or numbers.

scenes.narration_en: King Sejong's sundials were placed beside busy roads, at Hyejeonggyo Bridge and in front of Jongmyo Shrine, so that people passing by could gather and see the time.
scenes.illustration: A Joseon street scene: people in white clothes and a child gather around a sundial on a stone base beside a small stone bridge.

scenes.narration_en: On King Sejong's sundials, the hours were shown with pictures of the zodiac animal spirits instead of letters, so people who could not read could tell the time. Hoya cheers, because the tiger, 호랑이, is one of the twelve!
scenes.illustration: Twelve small, friendly zodiac animals (rat, ox, tiger, rabbit, dragon, snake, horse, sheep, monkey, rooster, dog, pig) standing together in a circle on a grassy hill; Hoya waves happily at the tiger; no letters or numbers.

scenes.narration_en: The sundials from King Sejong's time no longer survive. The ones we can see today were made later in the Joseon period, and several are designated Treasures, 보물.
scenes.illustration: Two elegant dark bronze sundials with fine silver lines, standing on cross-shaped bases inside a museum display case.

scenes.narration_en: Some are kept at the National Palace Museum of Korea in Seoul. Hoya peeks at a sundial in its glass case and asks his friend, "지금 몇 시예요?" That means, "What time is it now?"
scenes.illustration: Hoya and a child friend in a museum gallery, looking at a sundial in a glass case; Hoya has a curious, questioning face.

facts.claim_en: The angbuilgu tells the time by the shadow the sun casts inside its bowl.
facts.claim_ko: 앙부일구는 해가 만드는 그림자로 시간을 알려 준다.

sources.title: 보물 앙부일구 (Hemispherical Sundial)

episodes.notes: Makers deliberately not named: KHS entries list different makers (1985 Treasure: 장영실·이천·김조; 2022-1 Treasure: 장영실·이천·이순지) and encykorea says the maker is unclear (citing the Sejo Sillok, 이순지 led instrument-making). The Sillok inscription says '神의 몸을 그렸으니 어리석은 백성을 위한 것' (drew the bodies of spirits, for ordinary people); KHS and encykorea interpret these as the twelve zodiac animal spirits; narration follows them. Omitted: KHS's description of it as Korea's first public clock ('first' claim); line counts (KHS 1985: 7 vertical/13 horizontal; KHS 2022-1: 15-minute hour lines), because they vary by instrument; the sundial returned from the United States in 2020 (KHS 2022-1). Surviving Treasures date from the 17th–18th centuries (KHS). Theme set to 'nature' (sun, sky, seasons, zodiac animals); BP04 places Sejong science under Pillar E, so 'crafts' is an alternative. REVISION: 'seasons' replaced by 'time of year' (KHS: 계절선; encykorea: 13 절기선). Scene 5 now says explicitly that the animal-picture dials are those of Sejong's time (encykorea notes later versions used written characters). The reading of 'drew the bodies of spirits (신의 몸)' as the twelve zodiac animals is the interpretation of KHS and encykorea, not stated in the Sillok inscription itself.

episodes.title_en: Jang Yeong-sil and the Clock That Rang by Itself
episodes.summary_en: Hoya meets Jang Yeong-sil, the skilled craftsman King Sejong praised, and watches how flowing water, rolling balls and wooden figures made the Jagyeongnu water clock strike the time.
learning_goals: Recognize and say 물 (mul, water), 물시계 (mulsigye, water clock) and the sounds 종, 북, 징 (bell, drum, gong).
Know that King Sejong credited Jang Yeong-sil with building the self-striking water clock, which began keeping time in 1434.
Describe in simple steps how rising water moved balls and figures to strike the time.
Know that Sejong's original clock is lost, and parts of a 1536 water clock survive as a National Treasure.

scenes.narration_en: Drip, drip, drip. Hoya watches water fall drop by drop into a jar. "In Korean, water is 물," he says. "In Joseon, water helped tell the time, with a clock that rang all by itself!"
scenes.illustration: Hoya kneeling beside a large bronze jar, watching a thin stream of water trickle into a taller vessel below.

scenes.narration_en: Records say Jang Yeong-sil was first a gwanno, a servant owned by the government in Dongnae. He was so skillful that he took charge of craft work in the palace, and King Sejong valued his talent.
scenes.gloss_en: Jang Yeong-sil, a Joseon craftsman and inventor
scenes.illustration: A focused Joseon craftsman in plain clothes and a headband fitting bronze parts together at a wooden workbench, tools neatly laid out.

scenes.narration_en: King Sejong said Jang Yeong-sil had built a self-striking water clock, and that without him it could never have been made. The king decided to give him a higher official rank.
scenes.illustration: King Sejong in a red royal robe smiles and gestures with praise while the craftsman bows respectfully in a palace hall.

scenes.narration_en: The clock was called 자격루, 'the water clock that strikes by itself.' Water flowed from jars above into a tall vessel below, and a floating rod slowly rose as the water filled up.
scenes.illustration: Cutaway view: bronze jars set on steps pour water through thin pipes into a tall cylinder, where a rod floats upward.

scenes.narration_en: When the rod reached a mark, it set metal balls rolling. The balls moved wooden figures that struck a bell, a drum and a gong to tell the time: 종, 북, 징!
scenes.illustration: Three carved wooden figures in robes on a platform, one striking a bell, one a drum, one a gong; small metal balls roll down a chute behind them.

scenes.narration_en: From the first day of the seventh lunar month in 1434, the new clock kept time in a pavilion named Borugak at Gyeongbokgung Palace. Palace gates passed its sounds along so the city could hear the time.
scenes.illustration: A small palace pavilion beside a pond with a large pavilion behind it; a gate tower with a big drum in soft evening light.

scenes.narration_en: Sejong's original clock does not survive, but water vessels from a water clock made in 1536 remain. They are a National Treasure at the National Palace Museum of Korea. Hoya whispers, "시간이 됐어요!"
scenes.illustration: A huge plain bronze jar and tall bronze cylinders in a museum hall; Hoya stands small beside them, whispering with a grin.

facts.claim_en: A water clock measures time by the increase or decrease of water.

facts.claim_en: King Sejong stated that Jang Yeong-sil made the self-striking palace water clock (自擊宮漏) and that, although he followed the king's instructions, it could not have been made without him; the king then decided (his ministers agreeing) to add the rank of hogun for him.

facts.claim_en: In the Jagyeongnu, water flowed from upper vessels into a tall receiving vessel; a floating rod rose as the water collected, and at set marks it released metal balls that set the striking mechanism in motion.
facts.claim_ko: 자격루에서는 위쪽 물그릇의 물이 아래의 긴 물받이 통으로 흘러들고, 물이 고이면 떠 있는 잣대(살대)가 올라가 정해진 눈금에서 쇠구슬을 굴려 시보 장치를 움직였다.

sources.title: 국보 창경궁 자격루 누기 (Clepsydra of Changgyeonggung Palace)
sources.quote_or_locator: "맨 위에 있는 큰 물그릇에 넉넉히 물을 부어주면 그 물이 아래의 작은 그릇을 거쳐, 제일 아래쪽 길고 높은 물받이 통에 흘러든다. 물받이 통에 물이 고이면 그 위에 떠 있는 잣대가 점점 올라가 … 쇠 구슬을 구멍 속에 굴려 넣어준다. … 종과 징·북을 울리기도 하고, 또는 나무로 만든 인형이 나타나 시각을 알려주는 팻말을 들어 보이기도 한다."

sources.title: 자격루
sources.quote_or_locator: "1434년 7월 1일(양력으로 8월 5일) 경회루의 남쪽에 보루각을 세우고 그 안에 자격루를 설치하여 시각을 알리도록 하였다. … 살대가 떠오름에 따라 이 부력(浮力)이 지렛대와 쇠구슬에 전달되어 … 목인(木人)이 3명 서 있어서 하나는 시를 알리기 위하여 종을 치는 일을 맡고, 다른 하나는 경을 알리기 위하여 북을 치는 일을 맡고, 나머지 하나는 점을 알리기 위하여 징을 치는 일을 맡았다."

facts.claim_en: The Jagyeongnu announced the time automatically: wooden figures struck a bell (jong), a drum (buk) and a gong (jing).

facts.claim_en: From the 1st day of the 7th lunar month of 1434 (Sejong year 16), the new water clock was put into use in a pavilion named Borugak at Gyeongbokgung Palace; its sounds were relayed by drums and bells at palace gates so the city could know the time.

episodes.notes: Dating: the Sillok entry in which Sejong praises Jang and grants the rank 호군 is dated 1433-09-16 (lunar), while KHS and encykorea give 1434 as the year the clock was made/completed; narration avoids a making year and gives only the start of use (1434-07-01 lunar), on which the Sillok and encykorea agree. Other makers: encykorea's 자격루 entry lists 장영실·이천·김조 and its 장영실 entry mentions 김빈; the story names only Jang Yeong-sil, whom the Sillok (1433, 1434) and KHS credit. Location: encykorea says the 1536 vessels are at Deoksugung (outdated); KHS lists the National Palace Museum of Korea. Simplified mechanism: the Sillok distinguishes small copper balls and large iron balls and also describes 12 zodiac figures holding time plaques; narration says 'metal balls'. Jang Yeong-sil's later career and other instruments (e.g., 옥루, 혼천의) omitted.  REVISION: 관노 is described as a government-owned servant (Sillok 1434: 동래현 관노), worded neutrally; encykorea adds he was later freed and given a court post, so narration says 'first a gwanno'. Illustration of the 1536 vessels no longer shows dragons: KHS describes plain bronze vessels, and the only decoration mention found is an encykorea image caption ('수수통의 용문양'), which is not in the KHS text, so decoration is left out entirely. PASS 3: scene 3/f3 now say the king 'decided to give' the rank (Sillok 1433-09-16: 'I wish to add the post of hogun'; Hwang Hui and others agreed and 'the king followed').

episodes.title_en: Heo Jun's Treasured Mirror of Medicine
episodes.summary_en: Hoya learns how the royal doctor Heo Jun finished Donguibogam in 1610, a medical encyclopedia that valued staying healthy and wrote herb names in Hangul, now on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register.
learning_goals: Recognize and say 몸 (mom, body), 건강 (geongang, health), 약초 (yakcho, medicinal herb) and 책 (chaek, book).
Know that Heo Jun, a Joseon royal doctor, completed Donguibogam in 1610 and that it was printed in 1613 in 25 volumes.
Explain the book's idea that preventing illness and staying healthy matters before curing it.
Know that Donguibogam wrote herb names in Hangul and is on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register (세계기록유산, 2009).

scenes.narration_en: Hoya stretches his arms and legs in the morning sun. "In Korean, body is 몸," he says. "Long ago, a royal doctor of Joseon wrote a giant book to help people care for their bodies."
scenes.illustration: Hoya doing a morning stretch on the wooden floor (maru) of a hanok house, warm sunrise behind him.

scenes.narration_en: His name was Heo Jun, 허준, and he served as a doctor at the royal court. King Seonjo asked him and other doctors to write a new medical book. Today we call a doctor 의사.
scenes.illustration: A Joseon royal physician in official robes and a black hat bowing before a king seated in a palace hall; rolled papers nearby.

scenes.narration_en: When war broke out again, the work stopped and the doctors were scattered. Later the king asked Heo Jun to write the book alone, and gave him many medical books from the palace to study.
scenes.illustration: Heo Jun at a low desk surrounded by stacks of old thread-bound books, writing with a brush by lamplight.

scenes.narration_en: In 1610 Heo Jun finished the book: 동의보감, Donguibogam. 'Dongui' means the medicine of the East, Korea's own medical tradition, and 'bogam' means a treasured mirror, a model to learn from.
scenes.illustration: A neat stack of finished book volumes tied with cord, beside a round bronze mirror that softly reflects light.

scenes.narration_en: Donguibogam taught that staying healthy and preventing illness come before curing sickness. In Korean, health is 건강.
scenes.illustration: Hoya and two children walking happily through a pine forest, breathing fresh air, with a picnic mat of simple healthy food.

scenes.narration_en: To help country people use medicines growing nearby, the book wrote the everyday Korean names of herbs in Hangul, the Korean alphabet.
scenes.illustration: Gentle drawings of wild medicinal plants (bellflower, mugwort, a root plant) on a sunny hillside, with a woven basket of herbs; no writing.

scenes.narration_en: Donguibogam was printed in 1613 in 25 volumes. Later it was printed many times in China, and in Japan too. In 2009, UNESCO added it to the Memory of the World Register, 세계기록유산.
scenes.gloss_en: Memory of the World (UNESCO heritage list)
scenes.illustration: Rows of traditional thread-bound books on wooden shelves, with faint outlines of mountains and seas behind them suggesting the book's travels.

scenes.narration_en: Copies from that first printing are now National Treasures of Korea. Hoya hugs a book-shaped pillow and smiles: "보물 같은 책!" That means, "A book like a treasure!"
scenes.illustration: Hoya hugging a soft pillow shaped like an old book, sitting beside a museum case that holds a thread-bound book under gentle light.

episodes.notes: Sources disagree on the start year of compilation (KHS designation text and encykorea: 1596; KHS portal Memory-of-the-World page: 1597) and on its length (14 vs 16 years), so narration omits both. The number of royal books given to Heo Jun ('500여 권') comes from encykorea only, so narration says 'many'. UNESCO's page says 'compiled in 1613' (the printing year); KHS and encykorea give completion in 1610 and printing in 1613. Omitted: Heo Jun's exile to Uiju (1608–1609); the Jeongyu invasion is referred to only as 'war broke out again'. No remedies or medical advice are presented; prevention is described only as the book's stated principle. Herb names in Hangul: encykorea (compiling principles) plus 우리역사넷/신편한국사 ('모든 향약명을 한글로 표시'). Theme set to 'life' (body and health); BP05 lists 동의보감 at Pillar E (6.E4), so 'crafts' is the grid-aligned alternative. Scene 7 keyword changed to 세계기록유산 so 책 is not repeated. REVISION: the folk-tale entry 허준 설화 (E0063156) was replaced by the person entry 허준 (E0063152) as f1's second source. Birth year: DROPPED in pass 3. KHS gives 1539; encykorea E0063152 is internally inconsistent (infobox 1539 labelled 중종 32 which would be 1537, summary 1539/중종 34, photo captions 1546/명종 1), and other references give 1546, so narration and f1 give no birth year. PASS 3: added 우리역사넷 (신편한국사) as a second source for f4 ('Dongui' = Korea's own medicine, 集例) and f5 (prevention over treatment).

episodes.summary_en: Hoya opens the diary that Admiral Yi Sun-sin kept almost every day from 1592 to 1598, full of weather, feelings and everyday life, now a National Treasure and UNESCO Memory of the World.
learning_goals: Recognize and say 일기 (ilgi, diary), 매일 (maeil, every day), 날씨 (nalssi, weather) and 가족 (gajok, family).
Know that Yi Sun-sin kept a diary almost every day during the Imjin War (1592–1598).
Name things he wrote about: weather, his thoughts and feelings, family visits and ordinary people's lives.
Know that seven handwritten volumes survive, kept at Hyeonchungsa in Asan, and that the diary is a National Treasure and on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register.

scenes.narration_en: Hoya opens a little notebook. "Do you keep a diary? In Korean, a diary is 일기," he says. "Today let's meet a famous diary that a commander wrote long ago in Joseon."
scenes.illustration: Hoya sitting cross-legged on a floor cushion, holding a small notebook and a brush, smiling.

scenes.narration_en: Yi Sun-sin, 이순신, lived from 1545 to 1598 and was a commander of Joseon's navy. Before war came, he built ships and prepared defenses around Yeosu.
scenes.gloss_en: general; commander (Koreans call him 이순신 장군)
scenes.illustration: A calm Joseon naval commander in a robe and helmet standing on a wooden dock at sunrise, wooden ships moored in a quiet harbor.

scenes.narration_en: During the Imjin War, from 1592 to 1598, Admiral Yi kept a diary, writing in it almost every day.
scenes.illustration: Inside a simple wooden room at night, the commander writes with a brush by candlelight, a folded map beside him.

scenes.narration_en: He wrote about the weather, about army life, about his own thoughts and feelings, and about the lives of ordinary people around him.
scenes.illustration: Soft brush strokes on paper (no readable text) surrounded by little pictures of the sun, rain clouds, a fisherman and a farmer.

scenes.narration_en: He also wrote about his family and relatives, and about the people who served with him.
scenes.illustration: A warm scene at a coastal camp gate: a young family member arrives with a bundle and is greeted by the commander.

scenes.narration_en: Seven handwritten volumes of the diary survive. At first it had no title. Later, editors named it 난중일기, 'the diary written in the midst of war.'
scenes.illustration: Seven old thread-bound books with worn covers stacked neatly on a low wooden table.

scenes.narration_en: Today the diary is a National Treasure kept at Hyeonchungsa Shrine in Asan, and in 2013 UNESCO added it to the Memory of the World Register. Hoya picks up his brush: "오늘도 일기를 써요!"
scenes.gloss_en: I'm writing in my diary today, too!
scenes.illustration: Hoya at a low desk writing in his notebook with a brush; through the window, the curved tiled roof of a traditional shrine.

episodes.notes: Kept gentle on purpose: battles, the turtle ship (거북선), and Admiral Yi's death in the final battle of 1598 are omitted for young learners; the war is only named. Coverage dates differ by source (handwritten volumes: 1592-05-01 to 1598-10-07 lunar per encykorea; UNESCO and the KHS portal give January 1592 to November 1598, which includes passages known only from the printed 이충무공전서), so narration says only '1592 to 1598'. The KHS portal MoW page notes an eighth volume (1595, 을미일기) is lost; narration says seven volumes survive. The naming year (1795, 이충무공전서) comes from encykorea only, so no year is given. The National Treasure designation covers the diary together with letters (서간첩) and war-report drafts (임진장초). Romanization: surname written 'Yi' as in KHS and UNESCO usage (strict RR would give 'I'). 장군 is glossed as the customary Korean title for him; his posts were naval commands (수군절도사, later 삼도수군통제사). REVISION: removed 'even in very hard times' (not in any source); kept UNESCO's hedge 'almost daily' because the surviving volumes have gaps (the 1595 volume is lost). Scene 5 now says he 'wrote about' family, relatives and subordinates (two sources) instead of 'visits'. Second sources added for f3, f4, f5, f6 from 우리역사넷 (국사편찬위원회) and the KHS MoW page. episodes.title_en: Kim Hong-do's Pictures of Everyday Life
episodes.summary_en: Hoya looks closely at Ssireum and Seodang from Danwon's genre painting album at the National Museum of Korea, spotting a taffy seller, shoes that someone has taken off, and a sniffling schoolboy.
learning_goals: Recognize and say 그림 (geurim, picture), 화가 (hwaga, painter), 씨름 (ssireum, Korean wrestling) and 서당 (seodang, village school).
Know that Kim Hong-do (pen name Danwon, born 1745) was a Joseon court painter famous for genre paintings.
Describe what can be seen in the paintings Ssireum and Seodang.
Know that the album of 25 genre paintings is a Treasure kept at the National Museum of Korea, and that ssireum is living heritage today.

scenes.narration_en: Hoya dips a brush into ink. "In Korean, a picture is 그림," he says. "Let's look at pictures that show how ordinary people lived in Joseon!"
scenes.illustration: Hoya holding a brush over a sheet of plain hanji paper, an ink stone and water dropper beside him.

scenes.narration_en: Kim Hong-do, 김홍도, whose pen name was Danwon, was born in 1745. He was a court painter who painted many kinds of subjects, and he is especially famous for genre paintings, pictures of everyday life.
scenes.illustration: A Joseon painter in a light robe sitting on the floor painting on paper, brushes standing in a holder beside him.

scenes.narration_en: An album of 25 genre paintings, known as Danwon's genre painting album, is kept at the National Museum of Korea. It is designated a Treasure. In Korean, a genre painting is 풍속화.
scenes.gloss_en: genre painting (a picture of everyday life)
scenes.illustration: An open folding album showing small paintings of people working and playing, displayed in a museum case.

scenes.narration_en: Look at the painting 씨름, Ssireum! In the middle, two wrestlers grab hold of each other and test their strength. Around them, spectators sit in two curved groups, watching closely.
scenes.illustration: Two wrestlers gripping each other in the center, with two curved groups of seated spectators in white clothes and hats, one above and one below them, with round, cheerful faces.

scenes.narration_en: Can you spot more? A taffy seller, 엿장수, stands at the left, away from the crowd's attention. Over on the right, some shoes have been taken off and left.
scenes.gloss_en: taffy seller (yeot is a Korean taffy)
scenes.illustration: Detail of the painting's edges: a smiling taffy seller with a wooden tray stands at the left edge, apart from the crowd; at the right edge, a pair of shoes that someone has taken off rests on the ground.

scenes.narration_en: Now look at 서당, Seodang, a village school. The teacher and students are gathered around one boy, who has turned away, sniffling, while the other students grin and the teacher looks troubled.
scenes.illustration: A small schoolroom: a teacher in a square scholar's cap and several students gather around one boy who is crouched and turned away, wiping his eyes; some students grin, and the teacher looks puzzled.

scenes.narration_en: Ssireum is still loved today. It is a National Intangible Heritage of Korea, and in 2018 UNESCO inscribed traditional Korean wrestling as Intangible Cultural Heritage. Hoya rolls up his sleeves: "씨름 한 판 해요!"
scenes.gloss_en: Let's have a round of ssireum!
scenes.illustration: Hoya and a child friend in a sand ring, playfully gripping cloth belts and smiling, with friends cheering around them.

facts.claim_en: Genre painting (풍속화) depicts the everyday life of ordinary people rather than the royal court; Kim Hong-do's album shows the daily life and work of common people.
facts.claim_ko: 풍속화는 궁궐이 아닌 민간의 생활상을 그린 그림이며, 김홍도의 풍속도 화첩은 서민들의 일상생활과 생업을 담고 있다.

facts.claim_en: In the painting Ssireum, two wrestlers grapple and test their strength at the center, surrounded by spectators arranged in two rounded groups, one above and one below.

sources.title: 씨름, 《단원 풍속도첩》 (소장품번호 본관6504-22)
sources.quote_or_locator: "두 무리의 구경꾼들을 화면의 위아래에 둥글게 배치하여 가운데 공간을 연 다음, 서로 맞붙어 힘을 겨루는 두 사람의 씨름꾼을 그려 넣어 그림의 중심을 잡았다. 왼쪽에 서 있는 엿장수는 구경꾼들의 관심 밖에 있으면서도 이 원형 구도에 도움을 주고 있으며, 벗어 놓은 신발은 오른쪽으로 터진 여백을 좁히는 구실을 하고 있다."

episodes.notes: Attribution caution: NMK and encykorea both report scholarly debate about the album (differences in skill between leaves, retouching, many similar copies); some scholars regard leaves such as Ssireum and Mudong as genuine and weaker leaves as copies, and one view treats the whole album as a later model book. Only 13 of the 25 leaves bear the seal 김홍도인 (encykorea). Narration therefore calls it the album 'known as' Danwon's album and describes what the paintings show; the fact claim says 'attributed to'. The KHS designation text names the school leaf 〈글방〉; NMK and encykorea use 서당. Omitted: the switch (회초리) mentioned in an encykorea media caption for 서당; the album's purchase history (1918) and the 1957 remounting that separated two 군선도 leaves (NMK); Kim Hong-do's death (c.1806 per encykorea; KHS gives '?'). The 2018 UNESCO inscription was a joint inscription by both Koreas; this is not mentioned in narration. Scene 5 claim about shoes follows NMK ('벗어 놓은 신발'), without saying whose shoes they are. REVISION: (a) 'kicked-off shoes' removed; museum text says only 벗어 놓은 신발 (shoes taken off), at the right, narrowing the open space (NMK relicId=551); seller at the left, 'outside the spectators' attention'. 우리역사넷 says the shoes are the two wrestlers' and the seller looks into the distance; NMK's curator page says the seller looks outward, but narration stays with the museum's catalog wording. (b) Seodang layout softened to 'gathered around' because NMK says 둥글게 배치 around the boy while an encykorea caption says pupils sit side by side on both sides of the teacher. (c) Ssireum crowd: NMK says two groups arranged roundly above and below; narration says 'two curved groups'. (d) Quiz distractor for museum changed to other national museums.
